1.s: King Ahaziah of Israel, injured, sends to consult Baal-zebub, god of Ekron. Elijah announces his death and calls down fire on soldiers sent to arrest him.
1.d: Baal-zebub means “lord of flies”, possibly a mocking twist on Baal-zebul, “Baal is prince”; the name was later used for Satan [[tosn:2 Kings 1:2]] [[bible:Matthew 10:25]].

2.s: Elijah is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind with chariots of fire. Elisha receives a double portion of his spirit.
2.d: The “double portion” Elisha asked for was the Holy Spirit’s power at work in Elijah [[bsn:2 Kings 1:1–8:15]]. Malachi promises Elijah will come again [[bible:Malachi 4:5]], and Jesus applies this to John the Baptist [[bible:Matthew 11:14]].

3.s: Israel, Judah and Edom attack Moab. Elisha promises water, and Moab’s king sacrifices his son on the wall.
3.d: Moab rebelled by stopping its yearly tribute. The Moabite Stone (Mesha Stela) describes Israel’s control of northern Moab under Omri and Ahab [[tosn:2 Kings 3:4–5]].

4.s: Elisha multiplies a widow’s oil, raises the Shunammite woman’s son, cures poisoned stew, and feeds a hundred men with twenty loaves.
4.d: Feeding a hundred with twenty barley loaves foreshadows the miracles of Jesus [[tosn:2 Kings 4:42–44]] [[bible:Matthew 14:15-21]].

5.s: Naaman, an Aramean general with leprosy, is healed by washing seven times in the Jordan. Elisha’s servant Gehazi greedily takes payment and gets the disease.
5.d: Naaman’s healing led to faith: “there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel” [[tosn:2 Kings 5:15–16]]. Jesus cites him as a foreigner who was healed [[bible:Luke 4:27]].

6.s: An axe head floats. Elisha’s servant sees the hills full of horses and chariots of fire. Samaria starves under siege.
6.d: The horses and chariots of fire were spiritual beings, visible only when God allowed [[bsn:2 Kings 1:1–8:15]]. “Those who are with us are more than those who are with them” [[bible:2 Kings 6:16]].

7.s: Four lepers find the Aramean camp abandoned, and food floods into starving Samaria as Elisha foretold.
7.d: As Elisha foretold, food became plentiful, and the officer who doubted was trampled [[tosn:2 Kings 7:13–17]]. The lepers say, “Today is a day of good news” [[bible:2 Kings 7:9]].

8.s: The Shunammite woman’s land is restored. Elisha weeps as he foresees Hazael’s cruelty as king of Aram.
8.d: Elisha wept because he saw what Hazael would do to God’s people [[tosn:2 Kings 8:11]]. Judah’s kings walked in Ahab’s ways through marriage into his family [[bible:2 Kings 8:18]] [[bible:2 Kings 8:27]].

9.s: Jehu is anointed king of Israel and kills Joram, Ahaziah and Jezebel.
9.d: The watchman says Jehu “drives furiously” [[bible:2 Kings 9:20]]. Jehu, or perhaps his envoy, is pictured paying tribute on the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III [[tbd:001:Assyria, Assyrians]].

10.s: Jehu wipes out Ahab’s family and the worshippers of Baal, but keeps Jeroboam’s golden calves.
10.d: Jehu went beyond God’s mission, seeking power for himself, and Hosea later condemns his bloodshed [[tosn:2 Kings 10:11]] [[bible:Hosea 1:4]]. He ended Baal worship but kept the golden calves of Bethel and Dan [[tosn:2 Kings 10:28–29]].

11.s: Athaliah seizes the throne of Judah and murders the royal family, but baby Joash is hidden in the temple and crowned at seven.
11.d: Athaliah ruled from 841 to 835 BC [[tosn:2 Kings 11:3]]. Joash was the rightful heir to Judah’s throne [[tosn:2 Kings 11:4]], so David’s line survived as God had promised [[bible:2 Samuel 7:16]].

12.s: Joash repairs the temple with money collected in a chest.
12.d: Joash stayed loyal to the LORD while the priest Jehoiada lived, but turned away after his death [[tosn:2 Kings 12:2–3]].

13.s: Jehoahaz and Jehoash of Israel; the dying Elisha promises victories. A dead man touches Elisha’s bones and revives.
13.d: The dead man’s revival showed that Elisha’s promise of victory would come true for weakened Israel [[tosn:2 Kings 13:20–21]].

14.s: Amaziah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel, whose reign restores Israel’s borders as Jonah foretold.
14.d: Jeroboam II restored Israel’s borders as the prophet Jonah had said [[bible:2 Kings 14:25]] [[tosn:2 Kings 14:25]]. Pottery inscriptions from Samaria also show it was a prosperous time, the background to Hosea and Amos [[tosn:2 Kings 14:26–28]].

15.s: A string of short reigns and assassinations in Israel; Assyria begins to take territory.
15.d: In Judah, Uzziah reigned from 792 to 740 BC, a time of great prosperity [[tosn:2 Kings 15:1–3]]. In Israel five kings follow one another, most of them murdered [[bible:2 Kings 15:8-31]].

16.s: Ahaz of Judah sacrifices his son, appeals to Assyria for help, and copies an Assyrian altar for the temple.
16.d: Ahaz was one of Judah’s most wicked kings, even sacrificing his son [[tosn:2 Kings 16:2–3]]. Instead of trusting God, as Isaiah urged in Isaiah 7, he asked Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria for help [[tosn:2 Kings 16:7–9]].

17.s: Assyria conquers Samaria in 722 BC and deports Israel. The writer explains why: they worshipped other gods. Foreigners are resettled, mixing religions.
17.d: Samaria fell in 722 BC, Hoshea’s ninth year [[tosn:2 Kings 17:5–6]]. The writer explains it was because Israel “had feared other gods” [[bible:2 Kings 17:7]]. The mixed religion of the resettled peoples became the Samaritan religion [[tosn:2 Kings 17:40–41]].

18.s: Hezekiah of Judah trusts God, removes idols and rebels against Assyria. Sennacherib invades, and his officer mocks Judah’s God.
18.d: Sennacherib’s own records describe this invasion [[tosn:2 Kings 18:13]]. They do not claim Jerusalem was taken, only that Hezekiah was shut up “like a bird in a cage” [[tbd:008:Hezekiah]].

19.s: Hezekiah spreads the threatening letter before God and prays. Isaiah promises deliverance, and the Assyrian army is struck down.
19.d: The same story is told in Isaiah 36–37 [[bible:Isaiah 37:1-38]]. Hezekiah also built a tunnel to bring the Gihon Spring’s water safely inside the city walls [[tbd:003:Conduit]] [[bible:2 Kings 20:20]].

20.s: Hezekiah falls ill and is given fifteen more years. He shows his treasures to Babylonian envoys, and Isaiah foretells the Babylonian exile.
20.d: The visit of Babylon’s Merodach-baladan probably came during his exile [[tosn:2 Kings 20:12–13]]. Showing off his treasures was unwise, and Isaiah foretells that all of it will be carried to Babylon [[bible:2 Kings 20:17]].

21.s: Manasseh reverses his father’s reforms, rebuilds pagan altars and sheds much innocent blood.
21.d: Manasseh ruled from 697 to 642 BC and was the most wicked king of Judah [[tosn:2 Kings 21:1–2]]. The writer later blames the exile on him [[bible:2 Kings 23:26]]; Chronicles adds that he humbled himself before God [[bible:2 Chronicles 33:12-13]].

22.s: Young King Josiah repairs the temple, and the Book of the Law is found. He tears his clothes, and the prophet Huldah speaks.
22.d: The Book of the Law may have been all or part of Deuteronomy, or even the whole Pentateuch [[tosn:2 Kings 22:8–10]]. Huldah the prophetess gives God’s answer [[tbd:008:Harhas]] [[bible:2 Kings 22:14]].

23.s: Josiah renews the covenant, destroys pagan shrines across the land, and keeps a great Passover. He dies fighting Pharaoh Neco.
23.d: Josiah follows Deuteronomy’s command to read the law to all the people [[tosn:2 Kings 23:1–2]]. “There was no king like him before him… and there was none like him who arose after him” [[bible:2 Kings 23:25]], yet the judgement is not turned back [[bible:2 Kings 23:26]].

24.s: Babylon’s King Nebuchadnezzar takes Jerusalem in 597 BC, deports King Jehoiachin, leaders and craftsmen, and makes Zedekiah king.
24.d: Nebuchadnezzar II reigned from 605 to 562 BC and attacked Judah at least three times: 605, 597 and 586 BC [[tosn:2 Kings 24:1]] [[tosn:2 Kings 24:1–25:21]]. Ezekiel was exiled in 597 BC [[tbd:005:Ezekiel, Book of]].

25.s: Zedekiah rebels; Jerusalem is besieged, the temple burned and the people exiled in 586 BC. In Babylon Jehoiachin is released from prison and eats at the king’s table.
25.d: Babylonian records list the food given to Jehoiachin, and his kind treatment hints that God would one day bring his repentant people home [[tosn:2 Kings 25:27–30]].
